entries.title: Can one library borrow a book from another library?
entries.answer: Some libraries work together so their readers can use more books than any one library can keep. If your library does not have a title, it may ask another library to lend a copy. That is called an interlibrary loan. The lending library may send the book to your library for you to use, and the book goes back after you are done. Some things, such as very rare books, might stay where they are.
facts: Rules about what can travel depend on the libraries and the kind of item.

entries.title: How can a book’s index help you find a fact fast?
entries.answer: An index lists names and subjects in a book, often in alphabetical order. Each entry gives one or more places where the book discusses it. If you want to check what a book says about orcas, you can look for orcas instead of reading every page about the ocean. A table of contents usually lists whole chapters in the order you find them. The index can point to details within those chapters.
facts: Many books put the table of contents near the front and the index near the back.

entries.title: How can a library help people listen to a book?
entries.answer: An audiobook lets someone listen to the words of a book. In many recordings, a reader tells the story or reads the information out loud. People can pause and go back to a part they want to hear again. Libraries may lend audiobooks to many listeners. Some library services offer talking books and players for people who have trouble reading ordinary print, along with braille books for people who read by touch.
facts: The U.S. National Library Service provides audio and braille books to eligible readers.

entries.title: How can a library travel to its readers?
entries.answer: A bookmobile is a library that moves from place to place. It can carry books on shelves inside a bus or van and stop where people can come aboard. Visitors can borrow something to read and return it when the library comes by again. Places far from a library building can use this service, and a town might set up stops at schools or other places that people can reach easily.
facts: Mobile libraries can also travel in other ways, depending on the place and the route they need to reach.

entries.title: How can a museum see a hidden drawing under a painting?
entries.answer: An artist can sketch a plan on a surface and paint over it. Some kinds of light that people cannot see, called infrared, can travel through certain layers of paint. A camera made to catch infrared can show a drawing that your eyes would miss. With the right paints, the image can show how the artist changed a line or moved part of the picture while working.
facts: A picture made with infrared can help staff learn something while leaving the upper paint in place.

entries.title: How can a museum tell whether an object has changed?
entries.answer: Before an object goes on view, museum workers may look for marks such as a crack, a tear, or a loose part. They make notes or take a picture showing exactly where they found each mark. This report is a record of what the object was like at that time. Later they can check the report again. A little crack they notice might have been there all along, or it might be a new change that needs a closer look.
facts: A photo taken from the same angle can help people compare a detail before and after an exhibit.

entries.title: How can a recorded interview help people learn history?
entries.answer: In an oral history interview, someone asks a person to talk about events or a way of life they remember. The interviewer often asks when or where something happened, or for an example. A recording saves the speaker’s words and voice. Later listeners can learn what the person saw or felt. They can also compare that memory with other records, because people may remember different parts of the same event.
facts: A transcript gives a written version of an interview, while a recording lets a listener hear the voice.

entries.title: How can one museum lend a fragile object to another?
entries.answer: A museum can agree to lend an object for a display somewhere else. Before it travels, people who care for it check its condition and decide how it needs to be supported and packed. They may choose a box or crate that keeps the object from sliding or getting bumped. The two museums also agree about how the object can be shown and when it will come back. When the loan ends, staff can compare how it looks with the notes they made earlier.
facts: Some objects cannot travel safely even if another museum would like to show them.

entries.title: How did artists make some old books shine?
entries.answer: Some handwritten books have colorful painted pictures, large decorated letters, or very thin layers of gold. Artists could press gold leaf onto prepared parts of a page. Gold catches and reflects light, making part of a picture or letter glow when the page moves. This kind of decoration is called illumination. The writer and the artist could be different people doing separate parts of the work to make one book.
facts: Some illuminated books use brilliant colors for their decoration even without gold.

entries.title: How did people make a writing surface called parchment?
entries.answer: Parchment is a surface made by working and drying animal skin. To make it flat, someone stretches the skin tightly, then scrapes it until it is smooth and thin enough to use. Pieces can be cut into pages for a book. The result is different from paper, which can be made by pressing many loose plant fibers together into a sheet. Parchment pages can last a long time if people keep them in good conditions.
facts: Some medieval books were made with parchment before paper became common for books in those places.

entries.title: How does a call number show where a library book goes?
entries.answer: A call number is a group of numbers or letters a library puts on a book so people can find its place. Some parts can group books on similar subjects, and other parts help sort books within that group. You can find the number in the catalog, then follow the labels on the shelves. The same titles might have different call numbers in libraries that sort their collections in different ways.
facts: A label on a book’s spine lets people read the call number while the book is on the shelf.

entries.title: How does a library catalog help you find a book?
entries.answer: A library catalog is a list of the things a library keeps, with details that help you find them. You can look up a title that you remember, search for an author you like, or try a topic, such as oceans. A book’s catalog record can show which branch has a copy and what label to look for on the shelf. A record might also tell you whether the copy is out on loan.
facts: In older libraries, each title’s details might be printed on one or more cards kept in drawers.

entries.title: How does a library turn an old book into a digital copy?
entries.answer: A person making a digital copy of a book may use a camera or a scanner to capture images of its pages. The staff checks whether the words and pictures can be seen clearly and whether all pages are there in the right order. With a fragile book, they may support the cover and pages so the book does not have to open flat. The digital files can then let more people see the book while the original stays protected.
facts: A scanned page first gives an image of the writing, which may need another step to make the words searchable.

entries.title: How does a museum keep track of each object?
entries.answer: A museum can keep a record for each object showing what it is, where it came from if that is known, and where it is now. Staff give the object a number or code that connects it with that record. Two plain bowls may look almost alike, but their records can tell different stories. If one bowl moves to a display and the other stays in storage, the museum can update their locations without mixing them up.
facts: An object’s record can include measurements, photographs, or information about its maker.

entries.title: What does a library card do?
entries.answer: A library card often has a number or other code that connects to an account at a library. When you borrow a book, the library can use that account to record the copy and tell you when to bring it back. If you need more time, the library might let you renew the loan. Some libraries also use cards to let people borrow digital books or use other library services.
facts: The card helps a library keep track of loans. Different libraries set their own borrowing rules.

entries.title: What does it mean to put a book on hold?
entries.answer: If a library book you want is checked out, you may be able to put it on hold. A hold lets the library know you want a turn when a copy is ready. If several readers ask for the same book, they may wait in order. At some libraries, you can ask for a copy to be sent to a branch closer to you, where the staff sets it aside for pickup.
facts: The library may give you only a certain number of days to pick up a book that is on hold.

entries.title: What does the ISBN on a book identify?
entries.answer: An ISBN is a number that helps people identify a particular version of a book. ISBN stands for International Standard Book Number. If both a hardcover and a paperback version have ISBNs, they have different numbers. Both tell the same story, but the numbers help a shop or library request the version it needs. Two copies of the same version usually share one ISBN.
facts: An ISBN is often printed near the barcode on the back of a book.

entries.title: What does the U.S. National Archives keep?
entries.answer: The U.S. National Archives takes care of records made by the national government that have lasting value. Some are famous, such as the signed Declaration of Independence. Other records help people learn about their families or communities. They can look at old census records, maps, and photographs. An archive keeps evidence of what happened. Archivists organize these records so people can find them, and they protect fragile pieces from damage so future readers can study them too.
facts: Government records can be pictures, recordings, maps, or digital files as well as pages of text.
The National Archives keeps the original signed U.S. Constitution.

entries.title: What goes on behind the scenes in a museum?
entries.answer: A museum collects and cares for objects that can teach people something. A museum might hold paintings, historic clothing, fossils, or dried plants. Only part of a big collection fits in the rooms visitors can walk through. Staff also measure, photograph, label, and store objects so they can be found and studied later. A conservator helps protect fragile things. If a piece of cloth can fade in bright light, for example, a museum may show it only under dim light for part of the year.
facts: The objects a museum has gathered and cares for form its collection.
Researchers can study some objects that are kept in storage.

entries.title: What helps old books last longer?
entries.answer: Book pages and covers can wear out or change over time. Strong light can fade a cover, and a damp place may encourage mold. Libraries can place books in protected areas and support a heavy or fragile cover when a reader opens it. Some unusually delicate books are used only in a special room. Sometimes the library makes a copy so people can read the words without moving the original as often.
facts: Even a book that looks fine from outside can have pages that rip easily if they have become brittle.

entries.title: What helps you find one piece of paper in an archive?
entries.answer: An archive can keep a large group of records from a person or organization. A guide called a finding aid helps researchers understand what is in that group and where to look. It might list names on folders, when records were made, or how boxes are arranged. The guide can point you to the folder most likely to hold the information you want.
facts: A finding aid can describe a whole group of related records at once.

entries.title: What holds the pages of a book together?
entries.answer: The binding is the part of a book that holds its pages together. In one kind of binding, workers fold large sheets, gather some folds into groups, and sew the groups together near the spine. In some books glue holds the pages near the spine instead. Covers protect the pages, but the way a book is joined also matters. A strong binding lets the book open and close many times without its pages coming loose.
facts: The spine is the edge of the book opposite the place where the pages open.

entries.title: What is the Library of Congress?
entries.answer: The Library of Congress is a research library in Washington, D.C. It helps people in Congress find information they need and also makes materials available to the public. Books are only part of what it keeps. Its collections include maps, photographs, sound recordings, and music. A catalog helps people look up what the library has and where to find it. The library also runs a service that makes books available in forms such as braille and audio for eligible readers.
facts: The Library of Congress began in 1800.
Some library materials can be viewed online away from Washington, D.C.

entries.title: What makes something a primary source?
entries.answer: A primary source is direct evidence about the question you are studying. If you want to learn what a person saw at a parade, their own letter about it can be a primary source. The letter shows one view. Other people may have noticed something different. A photograph, a ticket, or the sound of an interview can also be a primary source when it gives direct evidence for that question.
facts: Researchers can compare primary sources to learn which details they agree on and which details still need checking.

entries.title: What makes something a secondary source?
entries.answer: A secondary source explains or interprets information somebody else recorded, saw, or made. For a project about the history of a park, a new book based on old maps, letters, and interviews can be a secondary source. It may help you see connections that no one old record shows. Keep your question in mind. The same book can be a primary source if you are studying how books explain parks today.
facts: Secondary sources may point readers toward original records they can check for themselves.

entries.title: Who frees a fossil stuck inside a rock?
entries.answer: A fossil found outdoors may come to a museum with rock still stuck around it. A specialist called a fossil preparator studies where the fossil meets that rock. Then they can slowly remove some of the rock using tools that fit the size of the job. Preparing a fossil can take a long time because cracks and weak spots are easy to miss. Sometimes staff make a support that helps the fossil stay in one piece as people study it.
facts: A partly prepared fossil can still give clues about how its bones sit inside the rock.

entries.title: Why are some bones in a museum dinosaur a copy?
entries.answer: A fossil cast is a copy that preserves the shape of a real fossil. Casting can help a museum show a bone while the original is kept safe in a collection. If only part of an animal was found, a display can also use copies from another specimen or shaped models to fill gaps. A visitor can compare the pieces and see how they fit. Labels can tell which parts are fossils and which are copies.
facts: An exhibit can make use of real fossils, casts, and models in one skeleton.

entries.title: Why are some museum rooms dim?
entries.answer: Light helps you see colors and shapes in a museum. Too much light over time can also fade dyes in cloth, paper, or paintings. Staff can use lower light, keep a case covered when it is not being used, or put an object away after it has been on view for a while. The amount of light an object can handle depends on what it is made of and how long it will be on view.
facts: Dim light can help a delicate object keep its colors longer.

entries.title: Why can one specimen matter when scientists name a species?
entries.answer: When scientists give a species a scientific name, a specimen or sometimes a group of specimens can help fix what that name refers to. These examples are called type specimens. A later researcher can compare other plants or animals with the type and ask if they belong to the same species. A type specimen does not have to look exactly like every other member of its kind. Its role is to keep the name linked to particular evidence.
facts: Collections may hold type specimens that have been studied and compared by scientists for many years.

How does a museum keep a specimen linked to its written information?

entries.title: Why do museum exhibits have labels next to objects?
entries.answer: A museum label can tell visitors the name of something, when or where it was made, and why it is in the exhibit. Imagine a smooth lump of stone sitting in a case. A label might tell you it was found beside a river and show how someone used it to grind food. Some displays use big text to tell the main idea and shorter labels to help visitors connect one object with that idea.
facts: A short label can help you notice something you might otherwise walk right past.

entries.title: Why do museums keep many objects behind the scenes?
entries.answer: A museum often has more objects than it has room to show at once. Staff keep many in storage, where researchers can still study them. A small bowl might sit on a support in a drawer, while a large statue may need a sturdy shelf or stand. Staff can record each location and check conditions in the room. They may also bring out different objects as displays change, so visitors see other parts of the collection.
facts: Storage can help protect objects from dust, bumps, or more light than they can safely handle.

entries.title: Why do we turn pages in some books and unroll others?
entries.answer: A scroll is a long piece of writing material that you unroll to read more of it. A codex is a book made from leaves joined along one side. The word is often used for old handwritten books. Each leaf can have writing on both faces. You can turn directly to a different part of a codex by opening it at that spot. A scroll lets you see more by rolling one end and unrolling the other.
facts: One leaf of a book has two sides, with one page on each side.

entries.title: Why does a museum keep dried plants on sheets?
entries.answer: A herbarium is a collection of preserved plants. Some plants are pressed flat and dried so they can be kept on sheets. A label can tell where and when a plant was found. The pressed plant can show details of its leaves, flowers, and stems to someone studying it later. If researchers compare several specimens from different places or years, they can ask questions about how the plants vary or when they flower.
facts: Researchers can study a pressed plant long after its leaves would have fallen or its flowers would have dried up outdoors.

entries.title: Why might an archive keep papers in their original order?
entries.answer: Papers can make more sense when they stay with the others that were kept with them. A letter in a folder might have a photo or an answer right behind it. An archive may preserve that order because it gives clues about how the person or group used the records. Anyone making a copy of a page can return it to the same place so the clues are there for the next reader.
facts: Sometimes the folder name itself tells researchers what the papers were about.

entries.title: Why might you read the caption beside an old photograph?
entries.answer: A photograph shows a scene from one point of view at one time. A caption or record may say when the photograph was taken, where it was made, and who made it. Those details can help you decide what the picture can tell you. For example, a photo showing a snowy street might turn out to be from another town. Sometimes the date or the names of people in the picture are still unknown.
facts: A caption gives useful clues, but researchers can still ask where its information came from.
